regular.q: Catherine wants to deploy a split-tunnel VPN. What is the key difference between a split-tunnel and a full-tunnel VPN?
choices: A split-tunnel VPN only sends traffic intended for the VPN client through the tunnel.
A split-tunnel VPN only sends traffic intended for the remote network through the tunnel.
A full-tunnel VPN makes the system appear as if it is on the local network.
regular.exp: In a split-tunnel VPN, only traffic destined for the remote/corporate network goes through the tunnel; everything else goes directly to the internet. A full-tunnel VPN routes all traffic through the tunnel.

regular.q: Derek is deciding between a full-tunnel and split-tunnel VPN for remote employees. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two?
choices: Full-tunnel VPNs only encrypt traffic to internal resources.
Split-tunnel VPNs route all client traffic through the corporate network.
Split-tunnel VPNs send only traffic meant for the corporate network through the encrypted tunnel, while other traffic goes directly to the internet.
Split-tunnel VPNs always provide stronger security than full-tunnel VPNs.
regular.exp: Same concept: split-tunnel only routes corporate-bound traffic through the tunnel; full-tunnel routes everything, which is more secure but uses more bandwidth.

regular.q: Michelle receives a drive that a manager retrieved from an employee's home and kept on her desk for a week before handing it to Michelle. What concern should Michelle raise if the drive is needed for a legal case?
choices: The drive cannot be safely copied after losing power for so long.
The drive may not meet legal hold requirements.
The drive may have lost data after losing power for so long.
There is a gap in the chain of custody for the drive.
regular.exp: Because the drive wasn't immediately secured, logged, and transferred with documentation, there is an undocumented gap in custody that undermines its evidentiary integrity.

regular.q: An investigator learns that a seized hard drive sat unlogged in a supervisor's desk drawer for several days before being turned over to the forensics team. What is the primary evidentiary problem this creates?
choices: A gap in the chain of custody
regular.exp: Any period where evidence isn't documented and controlled breaks the chain of custody, which can make the evidence inadmissible or questionable in court.

regular.q: Georgia wants a network tap that keeps traffic flowing even if it loses power during an extended outage. What should she deploy?
regular.exp: A passive fail-open tap requires no power to remain connected and pass traffic through. Active taps depend on power/backup power to stay open.

regular.q: A network engineer needs a tap that continues passing traffic with no active component or backup power if it loses electricity. Which type should be selected?
regular.exp: Passive taps are purely physical/electrical pass-throughs; fail-open means they default to letting traffic flow when unpowered.

regular.q: Marek wants to deploy a firewall that also provides antivirus/antimalware, VPN, and IPS. What type of device should he select?
regular.exp: A Unified Threat Management (UTM) appliance bundles multiple security functions into a single device.

regular.q: Which device consolidates firewall, antimalware, VPN termination, and intrusion prevention into a single all-in-one appliance?
choices: A next-gen firewall running one module
regular.exp: UTM = Unified Threat Management: one box, many integrated security services.

regular.q: Tom wants to duplicate all traffic on a network connection without adding load to the switch it passes through. What should he do?
choices: Use a tap while enabling port spanning.
regular.exp: A physical tap copies traffic independently of the switch's CPU, adding no processing load; port mirroring/SPAN uses switch resources.

regular.q: Which traffic duplication method has the least performance impact on the switch itself?
regular.exp: Taps are inline hardware devices that copy signal without involving switch processing, unlike SPAN/mirroring.

regular.q: Charlene set up a remote site with all systems needed to run IT infrastructure, but copies of data must still be brought there during an outage. What type of site is this?
regular.exp: A warm site has equipment ready but requires data to be restored/brought over; a hot site already has current data replicated and is ready immediately.

regular.q: A backup facility has servers, network gear, and workstations preconfigured, but the team must load recent backups onto it before it's fully operational. What kind of DR site is this?
regular.exp: Warm sites sit between cold (nothing ready) and hot (fully live/replicated) in terms of readiness and cost.

regular.topic: HSM vs TPM vs Secure Enclave
regular.q: Jim wants to centrally create, store, and manage certificates and cryptographic keys for his entire organization. What appliance-based hardware solution should he select?
regular.exp: A Hardware Security Module (HSM) is a dedicated network appliance for centralized key/certificate management. A TPM is per-device; Secure Enclave is Apple's device-level isolated environment.

regular.topic: HSM vs TPM vs Secure Enclave
regular.q: Which solution provides an organization-wide, network-attached appliance for generating and managing encryption keys and certificates across many systems?
regular.exp: HSMs are built for centralized, organization-scale cryptographic key management, unlike device-bound TPMs.

regular.q: Alaina configured switches/routers to use a private VLAN connected to dedicated management ports on her network devices. What type of management model is she using?
regular.exp: Using a dedicated management VLAN/interface separate from production traffic is out-of-band management, achieved through network segmentation.

regular.q: An admin dedicates a separate physical VLAN and interface solely for managing network devices, isolated from user traffic. What best describes this approach?
regular.exp: Segmenting management traffic onto its own VLAN/interface is a classic out-of-band management design.

regular.q: Christine has been notified that a firewall device has reached its end of life. What should Christine do?
choices: Immediately purchase a new device to replace it.
Begin planning to replace the device when a new version is announced.
Budget for a future replacement before end of support.
Plan to replace the device after end of support.
regular.exp: Best practice is proactive lifecycle planning: budget and plan replacement before end-of-support is reached, not reactively after.

regular.q: A network switch model is announced as reaching end-of-life next year. What is the most appropriate action for the security team now?
choices: Wait until end of support to begin the replacement process.
Begin budgeting and planning for replacement before support ends.
Do nothing since it still works.
regular.exp: Lifecycle management means planning replacements ahead of the end-of-support deadline, not reacting after the fact.

regular.q: Which of the following types of exercises is most similar to a real event?
regular.exp: A failover test actually shifts operations to a backup system, making it the closest to a real event; tabletop and simulation exercises are discussion/scenario-based only.

regular.q: Which of the following disaster recovery test types most closely mirrors an actual live event?
regular.exp: Only a real failover test involves actually shifting live operations, unlike tabletop/simulation/walkthrough exercises.

regular.q: Eve is investigating an incident where a user submitted an internal URL to a web application, tricking the server into retrieving sensitive data from that URL and displaying it as output. What term best describes this attack?
regular.exp: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) tricks the server itself into making unauthorized requests to internal resources on the attacker's behalf.

regular.q: An attacker submits a crafted internal-network URL as input to a web application, causing the server to fetch and return data from an internal-only resource. This is an example of:
regular.exp: The server making the unintended request to an internal resource on the attacker's behalf is the hallmark of SSRF.

regular.q: Which of the following is the least likely to be a threat created by having an unsecured wireless network?
choices: Spoofing the SSID to conduct an on-path attack
regular.exp: DDoS attacks aren't a direct/typical consequence of an unsecured Wi-Fi network the way eavesdropping, SSID spoofing, and unauthorized access are.

regular.q: An open, unencrypted wireless network primarily exposes an organization to which of these risks LEAST?
regular.exp: DDoS is generally not a direct consequence of weak wireless security compared to eavesdropping, spoofing, and unauthorized access.

regular.q: Kevin is attempting to determine whether he can destroy a cache of old records that he discovered. What type of policy would most directly answer his question?
regular.exp: A data retention policy specifies how long data must be kept and when it can legally be destroyed.

regular.q: Which policy would tell an employee exactly how long financial records must be kept before they can be legally destroyed?
regular.exp: Retention schedules (part of the data retention policy) define minimum/maximum keep periods for records.

regular.q: Bart wants to monitor for common types of anomalous behavior. Which of the following is not a common part of organizational security awareness and monitoring efforts?
regular.exp: Security awareness/monitoring efforts typically focus on risky, unexpected, and unintentional behaviors; 'repeated' by itself isn't a standard category.

regular.q: When categorizing user behavior for insider-threat monitoring, which of these is typically NOT one of the standard behavior categories examined?
regular.exp: The standard categories are risky, unexpected, and unintentional behavior -- not simply 'repeated' actions.

regular.q: Tina's organization is operating in a platform-as-a-service (PaaS) environment. Which of the following is a shared responsibility according to the shared responsibility matrix in a PaaS environment?
regular.exp: In PaaS, identity infrastructure is typically a shared responsibility between provider and customer, while data/accounts remain customer-owned and physical hosts remain provider-owned.

regular.q: Under a PaaS shared responsibility model, which area is typically split between the cloud provider and the customer rather than owned entirely by one side?
regular.exp: Identity infrastructure in PaaS often involves both the provider (platform-level identity services) and the customer (configuring and using them).

regular.q: Paul wants to monitor systems in his datacenter for unpatched, insecure services. What type of tool should he use if he does not have administrative access to all systems and devices?
regular.exp: A network vulnerability scanner can identify unpatched/insecure services remotely without needing local admin credentials on every host.

regular.q: A security analyst needs to identify outdated, vulnerable services across the network but doesn't have login access to every host. What is the best tool for this?
regular.exp: Network vulnerability scanners probe systems externally/over the network, so they don't require host-level credentials to detect many issues.

regular.q: Tara ran a port scan on a web server hosting her organization's public website and discovered that it is exposing ports 22, 80, and 443 to the world. Which one of these ports poses the greatest security risk?
choices: None of these ports pose a significant risk.
regular.exp: Port 22 (SSH) exposed to the public internet is the riskiest since it offers direct administrative/shell access if compromised or brute-forced.

regular.q: A scan of an internet-facing server reveals ports 22, 80, and 443 open to the world. Which open port is the greatest security concern?
regular.exp: SSH provides remote administrative access, so exposing it publicly is far riskier than standard web ports.

regular.q: Beena is the IPS administrator for her organization. The threat intelligence feed has provided information about a new attack the web servers are vulnerable to, and the servers must stay online. What can she do using her IPS to help the most?
choices: Manually create a signature based on the threat information to block attacks.
Provide trend information about attacks based on the threat feed.
Use behavioral information to stop traffic to the web servers.
Send alerts whenever a threat matching the new exploit is detected.
regular.exp: Creating a custom signature lets the IPS actively block the known attack pattern while keeping the servers online -- active prevention rather than passive alerting.

regular.q: A threat intel feed provides indicators for a new exploit targeting production web servers that cannot be taken offline. What IPS action provides the strongest active protection?
choices: Create and deploy a custom blocking signature based on the indicators
Log the traffic for later review
regular.exp: A deployed blocking signature actively prevents the attack, unlike alerting or logging alone.

regular.q: The Vice President of Sales has asked the IT team to create daily backups of the sales data. The Vice President is an example of a:
regular.exp: A data owner has ultimate accountability for a dataset and decides on requirements like backups, retention, and classification.

regular.q: A department head directs IT on how sensitive customer records should be classified and protected. This person is functioning as the:
regular.exp: Setting protection/classification requirements for a dataset is the role of the data owner, who is accountable for it.

regular.q: A company would like to orchestrate the response when a virus is detected on company devices. Which of the following would be the BEST way to implement this function?
regular.exp: Escalation scripting/automation (SOAR-style playbooks) can automatically orchestrate response actions when malware is detected.

regular.q: A SOC wants malware detections to automatically trigger isolation and ticket creation without manual intervention. What capability enables this?
regular.exp: SOAR-style escalation scripting automates the response workflow once a detection occurs.

regular.q: A company has been informed of a hypervisor vulnerability that could allow users on one virtual machine to access resources on another virtual machine. Which of the following would BEST describe this vulnerability?
regular.exp: A VM escape allows code on a guest VM to interact with the hypervisor or other VMs, breaking isolation between them.

regular.q: Which term describes a flaw that lets malicious code running inside a virtual machine break out and interact with the underlying host or other VMs?
regular.exp: VM escape is the specific term for breaking out of a VM's isolation boundary.

regular.q: A manufacturing company produces radar used by commercial and military organizations. A recently proposed policy change would allow the use of mobile devices inside the facility. Which of the following would be the MOST significant threat vector issue associated with this change in policy?
choices: Remote access clients on the mobile devices
Out of date mobile operating systems
regular.exp: In a sensitive R&D/defense environment, the biggest concern is data/IP exfiltration via cameras, storage, or connectivity on personal devices.

regular.q: A defense contractor is debating whether to allow personal smartphones on the factory floor where proprietary designs are visible. What is the primary security concern?
choices: Loss of intellectual property via device cameras or storage
regular.exp: The dominant risk in a sensitive manufacturing environment is IP leakage/exfiltration through personal device cameras and storage.

regular.q: Which of the following would be the BEST way for an organization to verify the digital signature provided by an external email server?
regular.exp: DKIM publishes a public key in DNS that's used to verify the digital signature attached to outgoing email.

regular.q: To confirm that an email claiming to come from a partner domain was actually signed and unaltered by that domain's mail server, what should be checked?
regular.exp: DKIM's DNS-published public key lets a recipient verify the message signature and integrity.

regular.q: A recent security audit has discovered usernames and passwords which can be easily viewed in a packet capture. Which of the following did the audit identify?
regular.exp: Plaintext credentials visible in a capture indicate an insecure (unencrypted) protocol like Telnet, FTP, or HTTP was used.

regular.q: While reviewing a packet capture, an analyst finds login credentials transmitted in cleartext. This is evidence of:
regular.exp: Cleartext credentials in transit point directly to the use of an unencrypted (insecure) protocol.

regular.q: An organization has developed an in-house mobile device app for order processing. The developers would like the app to identify revoked server certificates without sending any traffic over the corporate Internet connection. Which of the following must be configured to allow this functionality?
regular.exp: OCSP stapling has the server itself attach a timestamped, signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, so the client never has to contact the CA directly.

regular.q: A security admin wants to reduce the number of certificate revocation status checks clients make directly to the CA, while still validating certificates in real time. What should be configured?
regular.exp: OCSP stapling shifts the revocation check burden to the server, reducing direct client-to-CA queries.

regular.q: A company is accepting proposals for an upcoming project, and one of the responses is from a business owned by a board member. Which of the following would describe this situation?
regular.exp: A board member's ownership stake in a bidding company creates a conflict of interest in the procurement decision.

regular.q: During a vendor selection process, it's discovered that one bidding company is co-owned by the CFO's spouse. This situation represents a:
regular.exp: A personal/financial relationship that could bias a business decision is a conflict of interest.

regular.q: A company must comply with legal requirements for storing customer data in the same country as the customer's mailing address. Which of the following would describe this requirement?
regular.exp: Data sovereignty refers to data being subject to the laws of, and often required to remain within, the country in which it's collected.

regular.q: A regulation requires that EU citizens' personal data be stored on servers physically located within the EU. This requirement is best described as:
regular.exp: Legal requirements tying data storage location to national/regional law is the definition of data sovereignty.

regular.q: A user in the marketing department is unable to connect to the wireless network. After authenticating with a username and password, the user receives a message that credentials provided by the RADIUS server could not be validated against the root CA. The AP is configured with WPA3 encryption and 802.1X authentication. Which of the following is the MOST likely reason for this login issue?
choices: The user's computer is in the incorrect VLAN
The RADIUS server is not responding
The user's computer does not support WPA3 encryption
The user is in a location with insufficient wireless signal
The client computer does not have the proper certificate installed
regular.exp: An error about the CA/root certificate not being validated points to a missing or mistrusted certificate on the client, not signal, VLAN, or RADIUS-down issues.

regular.q: An employee gets a certificate-trust error when connecting to a WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X) network, even though the username/password step succeeds. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Missing or untrusted client-side certificate for the RADIUS server's CA
WPA3 not supported by the access point
regular.exp: A trust error after successful credential entry almost always points to a client-side certificate problem, not signal/VLAN/AP capability.

regular.q: A security administrator is updating the network infrastructure to support 802.1X. Which of the following would be the BEST choice for this configuration?
regular.exp: 802.1X typically relies on a RADIUS server that queries a directory service like LDAP to authenticate users/devices.

regular.q: To support centralized 802.1X authentication for wired and wireless clients, which backend directory protocol is most commonly integrated with the RADIUS server?
regular.exp: LDAP directories store the accounts RADIUS checks against during 802.1X authentication.

regular.q: Which of the following would be the main reasons why a system administrator would use a TPM when configuring full disk encryption? (Select TWO)
choices: Allows the encryption of multiple volumes
Stores certificates in a hardware security module
Maintains a copy of the CRL
Includes built-in protections against brute-force attacks
regular.exp: TPMs contain unique, burned-in cryptographic keys tied to the hardware and include anti-hammering/brute-force protection for stored secrets.

regular.q: Which of the following are core characteristics of a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) used for full-disk encryption? (Select TWO)
choices: Hardware-bound cryptographic keys unique to the device
Centralized management of certificates across the organization
regular.exp: A TPM's defining features are device-bound (burned-in) keys and hardware-level protection against brute-force key-guessing attempts.

regular.q: Sarah wants to ensure that email messages from their domain are verified for their authenticity and can't be tampered with, and that other sites know how to handle emails from their domain. Which protocol(s) should Sarah deploy?
regular.exp: SPF validates sending servers, DKIM signs messages for integrity, and DMARC tells receivers what policy to apply -- together they provide complete email authentication.

regular.q: A company wants to (1) confirm mail was sent from an authorized server, (2) verify the message wasn't altered in transit, and (3) instruct receiving domains on how to handle mail that fails those checks. Which combination accomplishes all three?
regular.exp: Each protocol covers one piece: SPF (sender authorization), DKIM (integrity), DMARC (policy/reporting).

regular.q: Isaac needs to sanitize an SSD that uses full-disk encryption and has been encrypted for its full service life. What is the most effective means of making the data on the SSD no longer retrievable?
choices: Completely overwrite the drive with binary 0s.
Reformat the drive using a full format.
Completely overwrite the drive with random patterns of binary 1s and 0s.
Destroy the encryption key for the drive and then use the SATA secure erase command
regular.exp: Cryptographic erasure (destroying the key) instantly renders encrypted data unrecoverable; combined with a secure erase command, it's the most effective and SSD-appropriate method.

regular.q: A company is decommissioning a self-encrypting SSD. What is the fastest, most effective way to ensure the data can never be recovered?
choices: Overwrite the entire drive with zeros three times
Destroy the encryption key and issue a secure erase command
Physically wipe it with a magnetic degausser
regular.exp: Crypto-erase plus secure erase is fast and effective for SSDs; degaussing doesn't work on SSDs since they aren't magnetic media.

regular.q: What is the virtual IP for a load balancer used for?
choices: It is the IP address used inside the load balancer to communicate with the load-balanced systems.
It is the front-facing IP address for the load-balancing instance.
It is the nonroutable IP address used for the load balancer that allows it to look like many systems.
It is the set of TCP ports used to allow systems to be identified behind the load balancer.
regular.exp: The virtual IP (VIP) is the single, front-facing address clients connect to; the load balancer then distributes requests to backend real IPs.

regular.q: Clients connect to a single published address which then distributes requests across a pool of backend web servers. What is this published address called?
regular.exp: The VIP is the externally visible address that abstracts away the pool of backend servers.

regular.q: Olivia wants to protect against DNS cache poisoning, and knows that digitally signing DNS replies from protected zones would be helpful. What can she configure to implement this capability?
regular.exp: DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records so resolvers can validate authenticity and integrity, preventing poisoning/spoofing.

regular.q: Which technology adds cryptographic signatures to DNS responses so a resolver can verify the data hasn't been forged or tampered with in transit?
regular.exp: DNSSEC specifically validates the authenticity of DNS data via signatures; DoH/DoT only encrypt the query transport.

regular.q: Which type of governance model uses a bottom-up approach where individual business units are delegated the authority to achieve cybersecurity objectives?
regular.exp: Decentralized governance pushes decision-making authority down to business units; centralized governance keeps it at the top.

regular.q: In which governance structure do individual departments set and enforce their own security policies to meet overall objectives, rather than following top-down directives?
regular.exp: Decentralized governance delegates authority to individual business units.

regular.q: The network that Jaime is connecting to requires each device to protect itself from potential threats both from outside the local security zone and from systems that share the same network zone with it. What security design concept requires this type of configuration?
regular.exp: Zero trust assumes no implicit trust anywhere, including within the same segment -- every device must verify and protect itself regardless of network location.

regular.q: A security architecture requires continuous verification for every connection, even between devices on the same internal VLAN, rather than assuming trust based on network location. This best describes:
regular.exp: Zero trust removes implicit trust based on network location, requiring verification everywhere.

regular.q: Jessica is looking for an informal mechanism to document the relationship between her company and an internal service provider offering a service to a customer in a different business unit of the same company. Which type of agreement is most suitable?
regular.exp: A Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) is an informal, non-binding document outlining mutual goals -- well suited for intra-company arrangements.

regular.q: Two departments within the same company want to informally document expectations for a shared internal service, without a legally binding contract. What agreement type is most appropriate?
regular.exp: MOUs are informal and commonly used between internal units rather than external contractual parties.

regular.q: Thomas has configured UEFI boot attestation on the servers that he is responsible for. What occurs during boot attestation?
choices: Each boot component is checked against a list of signed and known software before it is loaded.
The system builds a chain of trust from component to component as it loads during boot.
The system attests to a verification platform about the trustworthiness of the software it is running after it completes the boot process.
regular.exp: Attestation specifically means reporting/proving boot integrity to a separate verifying platform after boot completes -- distinct from secure boot (checking signatures) or measured boot (building a chain of trust).

regular.q: After a server finishes booting, it sends cryptographic measurements of its boot process to a remote verification service to prove it hasn't been tampered with. This process is called:
regular.exp: Attestation is the act of reporting boot integrity measurements to an external verifier.

regular.q: James, a customer service representative, frequently communicates with customers, handling queries and complaints. Which type of training would best equip him to handle social engineering and pretexting attacks he may encounter?
regular.exp: Role-based training tailors content to the specific risks of a job function -- customer-facing reps need pretexting/social engineering awareness specific to their role.

regular.q: A finance employee receives training focused specifically on invoice fraud and business email compromise, tailored to risks unique to the finance role. What type of training is this?
regular.exp: Training tailored to a specific job's risk exposure is role-based training.

regular.q: Andrea is reviewing a draft information security policy. Which one of the following statements would be more appropriately placed in a different document?
choices: All access to financial systems must use multifactor authentication for remote connections.
The company designates the chief information security officer as the individual with primary responsibility for information security.
The chief information security officer is granted the authority to create specific requirements that implement this policy.
The company considers cybersecurity and compliance to be of critical importance to the business.
regular.exp: Specific, technical requirements (like an MFA mandate) belong in a standard or procedure document, not the high-level policy itself.

regular.q: Which statement below is too granular/technical to belong in a high-level information security policy and should instead live in a standard or procedure?
choices: The organization designates a CISO responsible for security.
All remote database connections must be encrypted with TLS 1.2 or higher.
Cybersecurity is a critical business priority for the organization.
The CISO may issue supporting requirements under this policy.
regular.exp: Policies state intent and authority at a high level; specific technical mandates belong in standards/procedures.

regular.q: Tina recently identified that the organization is susceptible to an on-path attack. After review with her manager, they jointly decided that accepting the risk is the most appropriate strategy. What should Tina do next?
regular.exp: When risk is accepted, the decision and rationale must be formally documented for accountability and future review.

regular.q: After a risk assessment, leadership decides the cost of mitigating a low-impact vulnerability outweighs the benefit and chooses to accept the risk. What is the required next step?
choices: Formally document the risk acceptance decision.
Escalate to the board for remediation funding.
regular.exp: Accepted risks must still be documented for governance, audit, and future reassessment.

regular.q: Which one of the following environments is least susceptible to an injection attack?
regular.exp: LDAP, SQL, and XML all interpret structured command/query syntax and are common injection targets; a CASB is a security control, not a query-based data environment.

regular.q: SQL, LDAP, and XML are all common targets for injection attacks because they interpret structured input as commands. Which of the following is NOT typically vulnerable to this class of attack?
regular.exp: A CASB enforces cloud access policy; it isn't a query/command interpreter like SQL, LDAP, or XML.

regular.q: Sherry is concerned that a web application in her organization supports unvalidated redirects. Which one of the following approaches would minimize the risk of this attack?
regular.exp: Restricting/allow-listing redirect targets to trusted domains directly prevents open-redirect abuse.

regular.q: To prevent attackers from using a trusted site's redirect parameter to send victims to a malicious external site, what mitigation is most effective?
choices: Restrict allowed redirect destinations to the organization's own domain(s)
regular.exp: Only allow-listing legitimate redirect destinations closes an open-redirect vulnerability.

regular.q: Which one of the following situations would be described as Shadow IT?
choices: Using a product discontinued by the vendor
regular.exp: Shadow IT is technology/systems used without IT/security approval or visibility -- an unapproved repo fits that definition.

regular.q: A development team starts using a personal cloud storage account to share source code because the approved repository is 'too slow,' without informing IT. This is an example of:
regular.exp: Unsanctioned tools used outside IT's knowledge or control are the definition of shadow IT.

regular.q: Which one of the following tools is an exploitation framework commonly used by penetration testers?
regular.exp: Metasploit is a well-known exploitation framework used to develop and execute exploit code against target systems.

regular.q: Which tool would a penetration tester use specifically to develop, test, and launch exploits against a range of known vulnerabilities?
regular.exp: Metasploit is purpose-built as an exploitation framework, unlike the packet analysis, port scanning, or wireless-cracking tools listed.

regular.q: Garrett is attempting to manage the cloud server instances used by his organization. They do not currently tag cloud resources with the identity of the responsible individual. What is the primary risk of not better controlling this situation?
regular.exp: Without ownership tags, unused/forgotten VM instances accumulate uncontrolled -- this is VM/resource sprawl, an asset management problem.

regular.q: A cloud environment has hundreds of running instances with no owner tags or lifecycle tracking, many of which nobody remembers creating. This is best described as:
regular.exp: Uncontrolled accumulation of untracked VM/cloud resources is VM sprawl.

regular.q: Paul is the CEO of a large manufacturing company and wants reassurance about the effectiveness of the organization's internal controls while keeping costs down. Which type of audit should Paul consider?
regular.exp: An internal audit uses in-house staff, making it lower cost than external/third-party audits, while still providing management assurance.

regular.q: A CFO wants periodic assurance that internal financial controls are working, without the expense of hiring outside auditors every quarter. What audit type best fits this need?
regular.exp: Internal audits are performed by employees of the organization, avoiding the cost of external auditors.

regular.q: Kevin is using a service where a cloud provider offers a platform that executes his code in response to discrete events, and he is billed based on the actual resources consumed during each code execution event. What term best describes this service?
regular.exp: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) -- e.g., AWS Lambda -- runs code per-event and bills per execution; it's a more specific subset of PaaS.

regular.q: A developer writes small pieces of code that run only in response to specific triggers (like a file upload), with billing based purely on execution time and resources used. This model is called:
regular.exp: Event-driven, per-execution billing is the defining trait of FaaS.

regular.q: Which one of the following approaches, when feasible, is the most effective way to defeat injection attacks?
regular.exp: Allow lists (permitting only known-good input patterns) are more effective than block lists, which can be bypassed by unanticipated malicious input.

regular.q: Which input validation strategy is generally considered most secure against injection attacks because it only permits explicitly approved input patterns?
regular.exp: Allowlisting is the strongest approach since it defines exactly what's permitted rather than trying to enumerate every bad pattern.

regular.q: Rhonda needs a digital certificate for a new web server that she is putting online this afternoon. If she has no prior relationship with a CA, what type of certificate can she obtain most quickly?
regular.exp: Domain Validation (DV) certificates only require automated proof of domain ownership, making them the fastest to obtain.

regular.q: A startup needs to secure a new website with HTTPS today and has no existing relationship with any certificate authority. Which certificate type can typically be issued fastest, via automated validation?
regular.exp: DV certs are issued almost instantly via automated domain-ownership checks, unlike OV/EV which require manual vetting.

regular.q: Which of these threat actors would be MOST likely to attack systems for direct financial gain?
regular.exp: Organized crime groups are financially motivated (ransomware, fraud, theft). Hacktivists are driven by ideology, nation-states pursue espionage/strategic goals, and 'shadow IT' isn't a threat actor at all. NOTE: your source material listed 'Hacktivist' as the answer -- that appears to be an error; CompTIA objectives define organized crime as the financially-motivated actor.

regular.q: Which threat actor category is defined primarily by seeking monetary profit through activities like ransomware and financial fraud?
regular.exp: Financial motivation is the defining trait of organized crime threat actors.

regular.q: A security administrator is configuring the authentication process used by technicians when logging into wireless access points and switches. Instead of using local accounts, the administrator would like to pass all login requests to a centralized database. Which of the following would be the BEST way to implement this requirement?
regular.exp: AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) frameworks like RADIUS/TACACS+ centralize authentication for network device logins.

regular.q: A company wants all switch and router administrator logins authenticated against a central server rather than local device accounts, with logging of who did what. What framework provides this?
regular.exp: AAA centralizes authentication, authorization, and accounting for network device access.

regular.q: A company owns a time clock appliance, but the time clock doesn't provide any access to the operating system and it doesn't provide a method to upgrade the firmware. Which of the following describes this appliance?
regular.exp: A purpose-built, closed device with no user-accessible OS or firmware update path is a classic embedded system.

regular.q: A building's badge reader has no accessible operating system, no way to patch firmware, and runs a single fixed function. What best classifies this device?
regular.exp: Closed, purpose-built, non-upgradable devices are classified as embedded systems.

regular.q: An organization has received a vulnerability scan report of their Internet-facing web servers. The report shows the servers have multiple Sun Java Runtime Environment (JRE) vulnerabilities, but the server administrator has verified that JRE is not installed. Which of the following would be the BEST way to handle this report?
choices: Install the latest version of JRE on the server
Quarantine the server and scan for malware
Harden the operating system of the web server
regular.exp: Since JRE isn't actually installed, this is a false positive -- the correct action is to document and dismiss it as such after verification.

regular.q: A vulnerability scanner reports a critical Apache Struts vulnerability on a server, but investigation confirms Struts was never installed on that host. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Document and dismiss it as a false positive
regular.exp: After confirming the software isn't present, the finding should be documented and dismissed as a false positive.

regular.q: Which of the following is the process for replacing sensitive data with a non-sensitive and functional placeholder?
regular.exp: Tokenization substitutes sensitive data with a non-sensitive token that maps back to the original via a secure lookup vault.

regular.q: A payment processor replaces credit card numbers with randomly generated reference values that have no mathematical relationship to the original numbers, but can be mapped back through a secure vault. This technique is:
regular.exp: Tokens are non-derivable substitutes that require a secure lookup table to reverse -- that's tokenization, distinct from masking (partial obscuring) or hashing (one-way, no reversal).

regular.q: Which of these would be used to provide multi-factor authentication?
regular.exp: A smart card (something you have) combined with a picture ID for visual identity verification supports multi-factor style authentication; the other options aren't authentication factors.

regular.q: Which of these options actually contributes to multi-factor authentication rather than just access control or documentation?
choices: A smart card combined with photo ID verification
regular.exp: Only the smart card + photo ID combination represents authentication factors; the others are access control or policy, not authentication.

regular.q: A company's network team has been asked to build an IPsec tunnel to a new business partner. Which of the following security risks would be the MOST important to consider?
regular.exp: Connecting directly to a new external partner network introduces third-party/supply chain risk -- their security posture now affects yours.

regular.q: Before establishing a direct network connection (like a site-to-site VPN) with a new vendor, what category of risk becomes most relevant to assess?
regular.exp: Direct connectivity to a third party's network is a classic supply chain risk scenario.

regular.q: A company's human resources team maintains a list of all employees participating in the corporate savings plan. A third-party financial company uses this information to manage stock investments for the employees. Which of the following would describe this financial company?
regular.exp: A data processor handles data on behalf of and per instructions of the data controller/owner -- here, the third party processes employee data on the company's behalf.

regular.q: A payroll company receives employee salary data from a client business and processes it strictly according to that business's instructions to run payroll. The payroll company is acting as the:
regular.exp: Processing data on another organization's behalf and instruction is the definition of a data processor.

regular.q: A transportation company maintains a scheduling application and a database in a virtualized cloud-based environment. Which of the following would be the BEST way to backup these services?
regular.exp: Snapshots capture the full state of a virtualized instance at a point in time, making them the standard backup method in cloud/virtual environments.

regular.q: To back up a virtual machine running a database in a cloud environment, capturing its complete state at a specific point in time, what method should be used?
regular.exp: Snapshots are the go-to point-in-time backup method for VMs.

regular.q: Which of the following BEST describes a responsibility matrix?
choices: A visual summary of cloud provider accountability
Identification of tasks at each step of a project plan
A list of cybersecurity requirements based on the identified risks
regular.exp: A responsibility (or shared responsibility/RACI) matrix visually maps which party is accountable for which security functions, common in cloud provider relationships.

regular.q: In a cloud services contract, which document visually clarifies exactly which security tasks are handled by the provider versus the customer?
regular.exp: The responsibility matrix specifically maps out who owns which security function.

regular.q: A security administrator is implementing an authentication system for the company. Which of the following would be the best choice for validating login credentials for all usernames and passwords in the authentication system?
regular.exp: LDAP directories are the standard centralized store for validating usernames and passwords across an authentication system.

regular.q: An organization wants a single centralized directory service that authentication systems query to validate every employee's username and password. What should be used?
regular.exp: LDAP is the standard protocol/service for centralized directory-based credential validation.

regular.q: A company has created an itemized list of tasks to be completed by a third-party service provider. After the services are complete, this document will be used to validate the completion of the services. Which of the following would describe this agreement type?
regular.exp: A Statement of Work (SOW) itemizes deliverables/tasks a vendor must complete and is used afterward to verify the work was done.

regular.q: A contract specifies the exact deliverables, milestones, and tasks a contractor must complete, and will be used to verify the project was finished as agreed. This document is a:
regular.exp: An SOW defines the concrete scope of work to be validated against upon completion.

regular.q: A company is updating components within the control plane of their zero-trust implementation. Which of the following would be part of this update?
regular.exp: In zero-trust architecture, the policy engine (and policy administrator) sit in the control plane; the policy enforcement point sits in the data plane.

regular.q: In a zero-trust architecture, which component is part of the control plane, responsible for evaluating access requests against policy rather than enforcing the decision?
regular.exp: The policy engine makes the access decision (control plane); the enforcement point carries it out (data plane).

regular.q: A security administrator would like to monitor all outbound Internet connections for malicious software. Which of the following would provide this functionality?
regular.exp: A forward proxy sits between internal clients and the internet, allowing inspection/filtering of all outbound traffic.

regular.q: To inspect and filter all outbound web traffic leaving the corporate network before it reaches the internet, what should be deployed?
regular.exp: Forward proxies mediate outbound client-to-internet traffic; reverse proxies mediate inbound traffic to internal servers.

regular.q: A system administrator has configured MAC filtering on their corporate access point, but access logs show unauthorized users accessing the network. Which of the following should the administrator configure to prevent future unauthorized use?
choices: Remove unauthorized MAC addresses from the filter
regular.exp: MAC addresses can be easily spoofed, so filtering alone is weak; enabling strong encryption/authentication (WPA3) actually secures access.

regular.q: A network relying solely on MAC address filtering keeps experiencing unauthorized wireless access because attackers are spoofing allowed MAC addresses. What is the correct fix?
choices: Add more MAC addresses to the allow list
regular.exp: Since MAC filtering is trivially bypassed via spoofing, real encryption/authentication (WPA3) is the actual fix.

regular.q: A group of business partners is using blockchain technology to monitor and track raw materials and parts as they are transferred between companies. Where would a partner find these tracking details?
regular.exp: The distributed ledger is the shared, immutable record of blockchain transactions where all parties can view tracking history.

regular.q: In a blockchain-based supply chain tracking system, where is the shared, tamper-evident record of every transfer between companies stored and visible to all participants?
regular.exp: The distributed ledger is the core blockchain data structure recording all transactions.

regular.q: A company runs two separate applications in their data center. The security administrator has been tasked with preventing all communication between these applications. Which of the following would be the BEST way to implement this security requirement?
regular.exp: An air gap provides complete physical/network isolation, guaranteeing no communication path exists -- stronger than logical separation via firewall/VLAN.

regular.q: A requirement mandates that two systems must have absolutely zero possibility of network communication between them, not just filtered or restricted traffic. What architecture achieves this?
regular.exp: Only a true air gap (no physical network connection) guarantees zero communication; VLANs/firewalls are logical controls that could theoretically be misconfigured.

regular.q: A hospital's patient record system must ensure that lab results are never altered without detection as they move between systems. Which principle of the CIA triad is being prioritized?
regular.exp: Integrity ensures data is not modified or corrupted in an unauthorized way; hashing and checksums are common controls for it.

regular.q: An e-commerce site adds redundant servers across multiple data centers so customers can always complete checkout, even during a regional outage. Which leg of the CIA triad does this primarily support?
regular.exp: Availability ensures systems and data are accessible when needed; redundancy and failover are classic availability controls.

regular.q: A company wants to ensure that an employee who digitally signs a financial approval cannot later deny having done so. Which security concept does this address?
regular.exp: Non-repudiation uses mechanisms like digital signatures to prevent someone from denying an action they took.

regular.q: Which control provides proof of the origin and integrity of a message, preventing the sender from later claiming they never sent it?
regular.exp: Digital signatures bind a sender's identity to a message cryptographically, enabling non-repudiation.

regular.q: An employee logs in with a password and then must also tap a hardware security key. Which two authentication factor categories are being combined?
choices: Something you know and something you have
Something you are and somewhere you are
Something you do and something you have
Something you know and something you are
regular.exp: A password is something you know; a hardware security key is something you have. Combining categories (not just methods) is what makes it true MFA.

regular.q: A banking app requires a fingerprint scan in addition to a PIN before allowing a transfer. Which authentication factor does the fingerprint scan represent?
regular.exp: Biometrics like fingerprints represent the 'something you are' factor.

regular.q: A CISO compares the organization's current security posture against a target framework like NIST CSF to identify missing controls before writing a remediation roadmap. What is this process called?
regular.exp: A gap analysis compares current state to a desired state (often a framework or standard) to identify what's missing.

regular.q: Before pursuing ISO 27001 certification, an organization documents which required controls it already has and which it lacks. What activity is this?
regular.exp: Identifying the difference between current controls and a target standard's requirements is a gap analysis.

regular.q: A data center wants to prevent a vehicle from ramming through the entrance while still allowing pedestrian foot traffic. What should be installed?
regular.exp: Bollards are short, sturdy vertical posts designed to stop vehicle-borne attacks while not impeding pedestrians.

regular.q: A secure facility wants to ensure that only one authenticated person can pass through a door at a time, preventing tailgating. What should be installed?
regular.exp: An access control vestibule (mantrap) uses two interlocking doors so only one verified person passes through at a time, preventing tailgating.

regular.q: A security team deploys a deliberately vulnerable-looking server on the network, isolated from production, purely to attract and study attacker behavior. What is this called?
regular.exp: A honeypot is a decoy system designed to lure attackers away from real assets and reveal their tactics.

regular.q: To detect insider data theft, a company places a fake file named 'Executive_Salaries_2026.xlsx' on a file share and sets up an alert if it is ever opened. What is this technique called?
regular.exp: A honeyfile is a decoy file planted to detect unauthorized access; opening it triggers an alert since no legitimate process should touch it.

regular.q: Before a firewall rule change is implemented in production, it must be reviewed by a change advisory board, scheduled during an approved maintenance window, and have a documented backout plan. What process ensures this?
regular.exp: Change management governs how changes are proposed, approved, scheduled, and rolled back if needed, reducing risk of unplanned outages.

regular.q: A patch deployment fails and causes an outage. Because a rollback procedure was documented and approved beforehand, the team restores service within minutes. What part of change management made this possible?
regular.exp: A backout plan defines exactly how to reverse a change if it causes problems, which is a required part of formal change management.

regular.q: A security team wants only explicitly approved applications to run on corporate workstations, blocking everything else by default. What technique should they implement?
regular.exp: An allow list permits only pre-approved software/traffic and blocks everything else by default, which is more restrictive and secure than a deny list.

regular.q: Which approach to application control blocks a known set of malicious or unwanted programs while permitting everything else to run?
regular.exp: Deny listing blocks specifically known-bad items while allowing everything else by default -- the opposite approach to allow listing.

regular.q: Before a certificate authority issues a certificate to a web server, the server administrator generates a file containing the public key and identifying information to submit for signing. What is this file called?
regular.exp: A CSR contains the public key and organizational details, submitted to a CA to request a signed certificate.

regular.q: A company wants a single certificate to secure mail.example.com, www.example.com, and app.example.com without issuing a separate certificate for each. What type of certificate should they request?
regular.exp: A wildcard certificate (e.g., *.example.com) covers all first-level subdomains of a domain with one certificate.

regular.q: Two parties need to securely exchange a large amount of data quickly, so they use a single shared secret key for both encryption and decryption. What type of cryptography is this?
regular.exp: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both encrypting and decrypting, and is much faster than asymmetric encryption -- ideal for bulk data.

regular.q: A website uses a public/private key pair so that anyone can encrypt data with the public key, but only the server holding the private key can decrypt it. What type of cryptography is this?
regular.exp: Asymmetric (public-key) encryption uses a mathematically linked key pair, commonly used for key exchange and digital signatures.

regular.q: A database stores passwords by running them through a one-way function that produces a fixed-length value that cannot practically be reversed. What is this technique called?
regular.exp: Hashing is a one-way transformation producing a fixed-size digest; it cannot be decrypted back to the original input.

regular.q: To defend against precomputed rainbow table attacks on stored password hashes, a developer adds a unique random value to each password before hashing it. What is this called?
regular.exp: Salting adds a unique random value to each password before hashing, making precomputed rainbow tables ineffective.

regular.q: A company encrypts customer records stored on its database server's disk, even though no one is actively using them. Which data state is being protected?
regular.exp: Data at rest refers to data stored on media (disks, backups) that is not actively moving or being processed.

regular.q: An application uses TLS to protect customer data as it travels from the browser to the web server. Which data state does TLS primarily protect?
regular.exp: Data in transit is data actively moving across a network; TLS encrypts it during that movement.

regular.q: A government contractor labels a document 'Confidential' to indicate it requires more protection than 'Public' data but less than 'Secret' data. What is this labeling process called?
regular.exp: Data classification assigns sensitivity labels (e.g., public, internal, confidential, restricted) to guide how data must be handled and protected.

regular.q: Which data classification level would typically apply to a company's publicly published marketing brochure?
regular.exp: Public classification applies to information that is intended for open, unrestricted distribution.

regular.q: A security camera that records activity for later investigation, but does not stop an attacker in progress, is an example of which type of control?
regular.exp: Detective controls identify and record that an incident occurred; they don't prevent it from happening.

regular.q: A warning sign reading 'Premises under 24-hour video surveillance' is intended primarily to discourage an attacker before they act. What type of control is this?
regular.exp: Deterrent controls discourage attackers from attempting an action in the first place, often psychologically.

regular.q: A firewall ACL that blocks traffic to a specific port is an example of which control category?
regular.exp: Technical controls are implemented through technology/systems (like firewalls, encryption, and access control lists).

regular.q: A written security policy requiring annual risk assessments, approved and enforced by leadership, is an example of which control category?
regular.exp: Managerial controls are administrative in nature -- policies, procedures, and governance decisions made by management.

regular.q: A file server uses a RAID configuration that stripes data across multiple disks with distributed parity, allowing the array to survive a single disk failure. What RAID level is this?
regular.exp: RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity across at least three disks, tolerating a single disk failure without data loss.

regular.q: Which RAID level provides no redundancy at all and instead maximizes performance by striping data across disks with no parity or mirroring?
regular.exp: RAID 0 stripes data for performance but offers zero fault tolerance -- losing any one disk loses all data.

regular.q: A web application runs on two identical servers behind a load balancer so that if one server fails, the other continues serving users without interruption. What concept does this illustrate?
regular.exp: High availability designs eliminate single points of failure so a system keeps operating despite a component failure.

regular.q: Which metric describes the percentage of time a system is expected to be operational, often expressed in 'nines' (e.g., 99.99%)?
regular.exp: Availability, often expressed as a percentage of uptime, measures how consistently a system is accessible.

regular.q: A backup strategy captures all changed data since the last full backup every night, resulting in faster nightly backups but a longer restore process since every increment must be applied. What backup type is being used?
regular.exp: Incremental backups capture only data changed since the last backup of any type, requiring the full backup plus every incremental since to restore.

regular.q: A backup strategy captures all data changed since the last full backup, regardless of how many days have passed, meaning restores only need the last full backup plus the most recent one of this type. What backup type is this?
regular.exp: Differential backups capture everything changed since the last full backup, growing larger each day but simplifying restores to just two backup sets.

regular.q: A data center needs to keep servers running during a brief power outage while a generator spins up. What device provides this short-term bridge power?
regular.exp: A UPS provides immediate, short-duration battery backup power, bridging the gap until a generator can take over for longer outages.

regular.q: For extended power outages lasting hours or days, what is the primary long-term power resilience solution for a data center?
choices: An onsite generator with fuel supply
regular.exp: Generators provide sustained power for extended outages, while UPS units only cover the short gap until the generator starts.

regular.q: A well-funded group with advanced custom tools and patience to remain undetected for months is attacking a defense contractor. What attribute best distinguishes this actor from a typical opportunistic attacker?
choices: Purely ideological motivation with no capability
regular.exp: Nation-state and APT-level actors are typically characterized by high sophistication, significant funding, and persistence -- distinct from unskilled or opportunistic attackers.

regular.q: An attacker with minimal technical skill downloads a pre-built exploit tool from the internet and runs it against random targets without understanding how it works. What term describes this type of actor?
regular.exp: An unskilled attacker (formerly called a 'script kiddie') uses existing tools without deep technical understanding, unlike sophisticated nation-state or organized crime actors.

regular.q: An employee who was recently passed over for a promotion deliberately deletes critical files before resigning. What motivation best describes this attack?
regular.exp: Acting out of personal grievance against the employer is classic revenge motivation, common in insider threat scenarios.

regular.q: A state-sponsored group infiltrates a rival government's network solely to gather classified diplomatic communications, without disrupting or damaging anything. What is the primary motivation?
regular.exp: Espionage involves covertly gathering sensitive or classified information, typically for strategic or intelligence advantage.

regular.q: An attacker sends a text message claiming to be from the victim's bank, asking them to click a link and verify their account. What type of attack is this?
regular.exp: Smishing is phishing conducted via SMS/text message. Vishing uses voice calls, and generic phishing usually refers to email.

regular.q: An attacker calls an employee, impersonating IT support, and convinces them to read back their password over the phone. What type of attack is this?
regular.exp: Vishing (voice phishing) is social engineering conducted over a phone call.

regular.q: An attacker compromises or spoofs a CFO's email account and sends the accounting department an urgent request to wire funds to a new account. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: BEC involves impersonating or compromising a trusted executive's email to trick employees into fraudulent financial transfers.

regular.q: Which social engineering attack specifically targets finance or HR staff using a spoofed or compromised executive email account to authorize fraudulent wire transfers?
regular.exp: BEC is specifically defined by impersonating a trusted internal figure via email to trigger financial fraud.

regular.q: An attacker compromises a niche industry forum that employees of a target company frequently visit, planting malware that infects visitors' machines. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: A watering hole attack compromises a website the target audience is known to visit, rather than attacking them directly.

regular.q: Which attack strategy relies on infecting a trusted third-party website that a specific target group is likely to visit, rather than sending anything directly to the victims?
regular.exp: Watering hole attacks compromise sites the victims already trust and visit voluntarily.

regular.q: An attacker registers the domain 'gooogle.com' hoping users who mistype the real domain will land on a malicious lookalike site. What is this technique called?
regular.exp: Typosquatting registers domains that are common misspellings of legitimate ones to capture mistyped traffic.

regular.q: A company notices a nearly identical domain to its own, differing by one transposed letter, being used to host a phishing login page. What is this technique an example of?
regular.exp: Registering a domain that closely resembles a legitimate one to deceive users is typosquatting.

regular.q: An unauthorized person follows closely behind an employee through a secured door without the employee's knowledge or consent. What is this called?
regular.exp: Tailgating occurs when someone follows an authorized person through a secured entrance without their knowledge; piggybacking implies the authorized person knowingly allows it.

regular.q: An employee holds the door open for someone who claims to have forgotten their badge, knowingly letting them into a restricted area. What social engineering technique does this represent?
regular.exp: Piggybacking is when an authorized person knowingly allows an unauthorized person to follow them through access controls.

regular.q: An attacker watches over an employee's shoulder in a coffee shop to observe their laptop password as they type it. What technique is this?
regular.exp: Shoulder surfing is directly observing someone entering sensitive information, like a password or PIN.

regular.q: An attacker searches through an organization's discarded paperwork looking for printed passwords, org charts, or sensitive documents. What technique is this?
regular.exp: Dumpster diving involves searching through physical trash for sensitive discarded information.

regular.q: An organization's files are suddenly encrypted by malware, and a message demands payment in cryptocurrency to restore access. What type of malware is this?
regular.exp: Ransomware encrypts victim data and demands payment for the decryption key.

regular.q: Which type of malware is specifically designed to deny access to a victim's own data or systems until a ransom is paid?
regular.exp: Ransomware's defining trait is holding data or system access hostage for payment.

regular.q: A malicious program disguises itself as a legitimate free utility, and once installed, it opens a backdoor for the attacker. What type of malware is this?
regular.exp: A trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it, unlike a worm which spreads on its own.

regular.q: A piece of malware spreads automatically across a network by exploiting a vulnerability, without needing any user interaction or a host program. What type of malware is this?
regular.exp: A worm self-replicates and spreads across networks independently, unlike a trojan which requires the user to run it and a virus which needs a host file.

regular.q: An employee's computer is infected with malware that silently records every keystroke and periodically sends the log to an attacker. What type of malware is this?
regular.exp: A keylogger records keystrokes, often to capture credentials, and exfiltrates them to an attacker.

regular.q: Which broad category of malware is designed to covertly monitor a user's activity and collect information without their knowledge, such as browsing habits or keystrokes?
regular.exp: Spyware covertly gathers information about a user's activity; keyloggers are one specific type of spyware.

regular.q: An attacker installs malware that operates at the operating system kernel level, hiding its own processes and files from standard detection tools. What type of malware is this?
regular.exp: Rootkits embed themselves deep in the OS (often at the kernel level) specifically to hide their presence from normal detection methods.

regular.q: Which type of malware is specifically characterized by its ability to gain and maintain privileged (root/admin) access while actively concealing itself from the operating system and security tools?
regular.exp: A rootkit's defining feature is privileged, stealthy persistence that evades detection.

regular.q: A disgruntled system administrator plants malicious code configured to delete all backups automatically if his username is ever removed from the payroll system. What is this called?
regular.exp: A logic bomb is malicious code that lies dormant until a specific triggering condition (like a date or an event) is met.

regular.q: Which type of malicious code remains inactive until a specific condition -- such as a date, event, or user action -- triggers its payload?
regular.exp: Logic bombs are defined by their conditional trigger, unlike malware that activates immediately upon execution.

regular.q: An attacker systematically tries every possible password combination against a login form until one succeeds. What type of attack is this?
regular.exp: A brute force attack exhaustively tries all possible combinations until the correct credential is found.

regular.q: Which mitigation is most effective at slowing down an online brute force attack against a login portal?
regular.exp: Account lockout policies (or rate limiting/backoff) restrict how many guesses an attacker can make in a given time, slowing brute force attacks significantly.

regular.q: An attacker sends small DNS queries with a spoofed source IP (the victim's address) to open resolvers, which then send much larger responses to the victim, overwhelming their bandwidth. What is this technique called?
regular.exp: Amplification attacks exploit protocols where a small request generates a much larger response, directing that response at a spoofed victim IP to multiply attack traffic.

regular.q: Which characteristic defines an amplification-based DDoS attack as opposed to a simple flood attack?
choices: It uses a small request to trigger a disproportionately large response directed at the victim
It only targets a single specific port
It requires physical access to the victim network
It exclusively targets DNS servers and nothing else
regular.exp: Amplification attacks are defined by the response-to-request size ratio, multiplying the attacker's effective bandwidth against the victim.

regular.q: An attacker captures a valid authentication token from network traffic and reuses it later to impersonate the legitimate user without knowing their password. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: A replay attack captures and reuses valid credentials or session tokens to gain unauthorized access.

regular.q: Which mitigation best defends against an attacker capturing and reusing a valid session token later?
choices: Using short-lived tokens with nonces/timestamps that expire
regular.exp: Time-limited tokens and nonces make captured credentials useless shortly after capture, defeating replay attacks.

regular.q: An attacker sends more data to a program's input field than it was designed to hold, overwriting adjacent memory and potentially executing arbitrary code. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: A buffer overflow occurs when input exceeds allocated memory space, corrupting adjacent memory -- a classic technique for code execution exploits.

regular.q: Which secure coding practice most directly helps prevent buffer overflow vulnerabilities?
choices: Using allow lists for URLs only
regular.exp: Validating and enforcing input length/bounds prevents data from exceeding allocated buffer space.

regular.q: A standard user exploits a flaw in a poorly configured service to gain administrator-level access on a system. What is this called?
regular.exp: Privilege escalation is gaining a higher level of access/permissions than originally granted, often by exploiting misconfigurations or vulnerabilities.

regular.q: Which principle, if properly enforced, most directly limits the damage an attacker can do after achieving privilege escalation on one account?
regular.exp: Least privilege limits what any single account can access, containing the blast radius even if that account is escalated or compromised.

regular.q: An attacker manipulates a URL parameter with sequences like '../../../etc/passwd' to access files outside a web application's intended directory. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: Directory (path) traversal exploits insufficient input sanitization to access files outside the intended web root.

regular.q: Which mitigation is most effective against directory traversal attacks on a web application?
choices: Sanitizing and validating file path input, rejecting path-altering sequences
regular.exp: Proper input validation/sanitization of file paths prevents attackers from injecting traversal sequences like '../'.

regular.q: An attacker sends an enormous number of legitimate-looking API requests in a short period, consuming all available server resources and denying service to real users. What is this called?
regular.exp: Resource exhaustion attacks overwhelm a system's finite resources (CPU, memory, connections) to cause denial of service.

regular.q: Which API security control is most effective at preventing a single client from exhausting server resources with excessive requests?
regular.exp: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a given period, directly mitigating resource exhaustion.

regular.q: An attacker intercepts a connection negotiation and forces the client and server to use an older, weaker encryption protocol that can be more easily broken. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: A downgrade attack forces a connection to use a weaker, more vulnerable protocol or cipher version than it would otherwise negotiate.

regular.q: Which practice best prevents downgrade attacks against a web server's TLS configuration?
choices: Disabling support for outdated/weak protocol versions and ciphers
regular.exp: Explicitly disabling deprecated, weak protocol versions prevents an attacker from forcing a downgrade to something exploitable.

regular.q: A researcher finds two different input files that produce the identical hash digest, undermining the hash function's integrity guarantee. What is this called?
regular.exp: A hash collision occurs when two different inputs produce the same hash output, which can undermine integrity checks and digital signatures if exploitable.

regular.q: Which type of attack exploits the probability principle that finding any two matching values among a set is statistically easier than finding a match to one specific value?
regular.exp: The birthday attack leverages probability theory (the 'birthday paradox') to find hash collisions faster than brute force would suggest.

regular.q: An attacker uses a precomputed table of hash values mapped to their plaintext inputs to quickly reverse a stolen, unsalted password hash. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: Rainbow tables are precomputed hash-to-plaintext lookup tables that speed up cracking unsalted hashed passwords.

regular.q: Which single control most directly neutralizes the effectiveness of rainbow table attacks against stored password hashes?
regular.exp: Salting makes precomputed rainbow tables useless because each password now hashes to a unique value even if the passwords are identical.

regular.q: Instead of trying many passwords against one account, an attacker tries one common password (like 'Summer2026!') against thousands of different accounts to avoid triggering lockout policies. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: Password spraying tries a small number of common passwords across many accounts, staying under per-account lockout thresholds.

regular.q: Which detection approach is most effective at spotting a password spraying campaign that a standard per-account lockout policy would miss?
choices: Monitoring for many accounts having a small number of failed logins with the same password pattern, org-wide
Watching a single account for many failed logins
Disabling all logging to reduce noise
regular.exp: Because password spraying spreads attempts thin across many accounts, org-wide correlation (not single-account monitoring) is needed to catch it.

regular.q: A user's account logs in from New York and, twelve minutes later, logs in again from a country on another continent. What indicator of compromise does this represent?
regular.exp: Impossible travel flags logins from geographically distant locations in a timeframe that would be physically impossible to travel between.

regular.q: Which type of security alert is triggered when authentication logs show a user account accessing resources from two locations too far apart to reach in the elapsed time?
regular.exp: This is the definition of an impossible travel indicator of compromise, often used by SIEM/UEBA tools to flag likely account compromise.

regular.q: A system administrator disables unused services, closes unnecessary ports, changes default credentials, and removes unneeded software from a newly deployed server. What is this process called?
regular.exp: Hardening reduces a system's attack surface by disabling unnecessary features, services, and accounts, and enforcing secure configurations.

regular.q: Which hardening action most directly reduces a server's attack surface by eliminating an entire class of potential entry points?
regular.exp: Turning off unused ports/services removes potential attack vectors entirely, rather than just detecting or slowing an attack after the fact.

regular.q: A hospital and its regional partner clinics share a single cloud environment built specifically for healthcare organizations with common compliance needs, not open to the general public. What cloud deployment model is this?
regular.exp: A community cloud is shared by several organizations with common concerns (like compliance requirements), distinct from a single-tenant private cloud or the general-access public cloud.

regular.q: A company keeps sensitive financial data in an on-premises data center but bursts overflow web traffic to a public cloud provider during peak season. What cloud deployment model is this?
regular.exp: A hybrid cloud combines private/on-premises infrastructure with public cloud resources, integrated to work together.

regular.q: A DevOps team defines all of their servers, networks, and security groups in version-controlled configuration files that automatically provision identical environments every time. What practice is this?
regular.exp: IaC manages and provisions infrastructure through machine-readable definition files rather than manual configuration, improving consistency and repeatability.

regular.q: Which benefit is most directly associated with using Infrastructure as Code for deploying cloud environments?
choices: Elimination of the need for any access controls
Guaranteed compliance with all regulations automatically
Removal of the need for vulnerability scanning
regular.exp: IaC's core benefit is consistent, auditable, repeatable infrastructure deployment defined in code rather than manual, error-prone processes.

regular.q: An application is broken into many small, independently deployable services that each handle one specific function and communicate over APIs, rather than being built as one large monolithic program. What architecture is this?
regular.exp: Microservices architecture decomposes an application into small, independently deployable services, improving scalability and fault isolation but increasing API attack surface.

regular.q: What is a notable security tradeoff of adopting a microservices architecture compared to a monolithic application?
choices: A larger overall attack surface due to many inter-service APIs
No need for authentication between services
